content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Snack is a specially formulated light snack for children aged 6 months to 3 years. It is made from whole‑grain flakes, fruit puree, and natural vitamins, and contains no artificial colors, flavors, or preservatives.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The snack comes in small stick shapes that are easy for tiny hands to grasp.
It includes fermented probiotics that support a healthy gut microbiome.
Each serving provides 15% of the daily recommended iron for this age group.
The product has been dermatologically tested to be free of common allergens except milk protein.
Packaging is made from biodegradable material, safe for the environment.

items.title: Supports bone growth
items.content: Contains calcium and vitamin D, essential for developing strong bones in toddlers.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Vitamin C and zinc help protect against common colds and infections.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Probiotics and dietary fiber promote regular bowel movements and prevent constipation.

items.title: Provides steady energy
items.content: A blend of slow‑release carbohydrates offers stable energy without sharp blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Reduces allergy risk
items.content: Free from nuts, soy, and gluten, lowering the chance of food‑related allergies.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: The snack contains milk protein; children with known allergy should avoid it.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Small pieces may pose a choking risk for children under 12 months; offer only after 12 months under supervision.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although reduced, children prone to cavities should have limited portions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The snack can be given as a standalone bite between meals. For children under 12 months, crush the sticks into fine crumbs and mix with puree. For older toddlers, serve the sticks whole, allowing the child to hold and eat them independently.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed package. After opening, use within 30 days. Discard if any moldy odor or off‑taste develops.

content.title: About
content.content: Beef tenderloin is a lean, buttery‑textured cut taken from the lumbar region of the cow. It is prized for its tenderness, low fat content, and rich beef flavor. Tenderloin is commonly used for steaks because it cooks quickly and stays juicy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tenderloin is the most tender beef cut, often compared to chicken breast in softness.
It is traditionally cooked on a grill or in a hot skillet to highlight its natural flavor.
Different countries have their own names: in the US it’s called “tenderloin steak,” in France “filet de bœuf.”
For the perfect steak, let the tenderloin sit at room temperature for 30‑40 minutes before cooking.
Beef tenderloin is high in protein and iron but low in connective tissue.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Tenderloin provides about 22 g of high‑quality protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: High iron content
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: Tenderloin has one of the lowest fat levels among beef cuts, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are essential for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Creatine and carnosine
items.content: These compounds help improve physical performance and have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Although lean, tenderloin still contains cholesterol, so people with hypercholesterolemia should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor pathogens such as E. coli. Cook steaks to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals can have an allergic reaction to beef.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Beef is high in purines, which can exacerbate gout symptoms in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tenderloin is best cooked over high heat: grilling, pan‑searing, or broiling. Season with salt and pepper, sear each side for a few minutes, then let rest 5‑10 minutes so juices redistribute.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh tenderloin in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C, wrapped in plastic film or an airtight container, for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C in a vacuum‑sealed bag; it will keep well for up to 6 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Beer is an alcoholic beverage produced by fermenting malted grains (such as barley or wheat) with water, hops, and yeast. It comes in a wide range of styles, from light lagers to rich stouts, and is one of the most popular drinks worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beer is considered one of the oldest drinks, with archaeological evidence dating back to 5,000 BCE.
Hops are added not only for bitterness but also as a natural preservative.
There are more than 20,000 beer styles, classified by flavor, region, and brewing method.
In many countries, beer is served in specially shaped glasses that enhance aroma and taste.
Beer festivals such as Germany's Oktoberfest attract millions of visitors each year.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Beer is a good source of B1, B2, B6, and folate, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: It provides magnesium, potassium, phosphorus, and selenium, important for muscle and bone health.

items.title: Polysaccharides and fiber
items.content: Malt and hops contain soluble fibers that may benefit digestive health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids from hops have antioxidant properties that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Moderate consumption and cardiovascular health
items.content: Some studies associate moderate beer intake with a slightly reduced risk of heart disease.

items.title: Alcohol content
items.content: Beer contains alcohol and should be consumed in moderation; excessive intake leads to health problems.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Certain beers, especially sweet or high‑ABV varieties, can be high in calories and may contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Yeast or gluten allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to yeast or gluten present in barley malt.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Alcohol can amplify the effects of many drugs, so people on medication should limit beer consumption.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Beer is typically served chilled in glasses or mugs suited to its style. Pairings include light lagers with seafood and salads, ales with meat and cheese, and stouts with desserts or chocolate.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store beer in a cool, dark place, ideally at 7‑12 °C (45‑54 °F). Avoid direct sunlight, which can cause "skunking" and degrade flavor. Once opened, seal the bottle or keg and consume within a few days.

content.title: About
content.content: Decaffeinated nonfat iced latte is a cold beverage made from espresso, diluted with low‑fat milk and lightly sweetened. The coffee undergoes a decaffeination process that retains aroma, while the nonfat milk keeps the drink light and low‑calorie.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Decaffeination is usually done by water or carbon‑filter methods, removing almost all caffeine without losing flavor.
Iced latte originated in the United States in the 1990s as a summer variant of the classic latte.
Nonfat milk retains most of the protein and calcium but contains virtually no fat.
Decaf coffee may still contain up to 0.1% caffeine, which can affect very sensitive individuals.
Cold coffee is often perceived as more refreshing in hot weather than hot coffee.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Decaffeinated coffee keeps polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports hydration
items.content: A cold, water‑rich drink contributes to overall fluid balance.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Nonfat milk is a good source of calcium, essential for bone health.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: The absence of fat makes the latte less caloric than a regular latte.

items.title: May aid focus
items.content: The small remaining caffeine amount can improve alertness without strong stimulation.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Even trace caffeine may trigger reactions in highly sensitive people.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Nonfat milk contains lactose; those with intolerance should choose alternatives.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: Some iced latte versions include sweeteners that increase calorie content.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Coffee can raise stomach acidity, which may be problematic for gastritis sufferers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the decaf iced latte cold over ice, optionally add a splash of vanilla syrup or stevia. You can garnish with nonfat whipped cream or a sprinkle of cinnamon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared drink refrigerated and consume within 24 hours. Store nonfat milk in its original sealed container at 1‑4 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Fried crayfish is a dish made from freshwater crayfish that are pan‑fried until golden and crispy. The meat is tender, slightly sweet, and carries a distinct seafood aroma. It is commonly served as an appetizer or a hot main course in restaurants and at outdoor gatherings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Crayfish belong to the order Decapoda and can thrive in both fresh and mildly brackish waters.
In Russia and many CIS countries, fried crayfish is considered a delicacy, especially in regions with strong fishing traditions.
Crayfish meat is high in protein and contains all essential amino acids.
Traditionally, crayfish are fried in butter or vegetable oil with garlic and spices.
The main harvesting season for crayfish is summer through early autumn.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Crayfish provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many seafood items, crayfish contains little saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for healthy blood formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Crayfish is a good source of zinc, iron, and magnesium, which aid immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Small amounts of omega‑3s help support heart health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to crayfish proteins.

items.title: Parasites and toxins
items.content: Raw or undercooked crayfish can harbor parasites; thorough frying is essential.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: While low in fat, crayfish does contain cholesterol, so people with hypercholesterolemia should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Crayfish from polluted waters may accumulate cadmium or lead; choose products from reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fried crayfish is typically served hot, sprinkled with salt, paprika, or a squeeze of lemon. It can be eaten by hand, pulling off the tail and legs, or incorporated into salads, pastas, and rice dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fried crayfish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a tightly sealed bag for up to 3 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Fried okra consists of sliced young pods of the okra plant (Abelmoschus esculentus) that are deep‑fried in vegetable oil until golden and crisp. The vegetable has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a crunchy texture. It is commonly served as a snack, side dish, or topping in Southern U.S., Caribbean, and Southeast Asian cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Okra is also known as "lady’s fingers" in many English‑speaking regions.
In the Southern United States, fried okra is a staple at state fairs and family gatherings.
The mucilaginous (slimy) compounds in okra help keep the fried coating moist and flavorful.
Okra seeds are pressed to produce okra oil, while the young pods are used in soups, stews, and gumbo.
Traditional African recipes often fry okra with spices such as paprika, garlic, and cayenne.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Okra provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and regularity.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A 100‑g serving of fried okra contains roughly 150 kcal, making it a relatively light snack when portioned.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: It supplies thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Mineral source
items.content: Okra contains potassium, magnesium, and iron, contributing to electrolyte balance and blood health.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols in okra help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to okra, ranging from skin rash to swelling.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Okra contains oxalates, which in high amounts can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

items.title: Frying oil
items.content: Frequent consumption of deep‑fried foods can increase intake of unhealthy fats and trans‑fatty acids.

items.title: Digestive sensitivity
items.content: The mucilage may cause stomach discomfort in people with sensitive digestion.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fried okra can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, seasoned with salt, paprika, or Cajun spices. It is also added to salads, tacos, burgers, and soups. For extra crunch, the pods are often lightly coated in cornmeal before frying.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fried okra in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3‑4 days. For longer shelf life, keep it refrigerated, where it will stay crisp for about a week.

content.title: About
content.content: Mustard greens (Brassica juncea) are edible young leaves and stems of the plant, widely used in Asian cuisine. They have a mildly bitter, peppery flavor and a crunchy texture. Raw greens are often added to salads, smoothies, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mustard greens belong to the cruciferous family, along with broccoli, cabbage, and turnip.
In traditional Chinese medicine they are used to aid digestion.
High levels of glucosinolates give the leaves their distinctive sharp aroma.
In Japan, mustard greens are frequently pickled in soy sauce and rice vinegar.
Raw leaves are a rich source of vitamin K, important for blood clotting.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for normal blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains vitamins A and C
items.content: These vitamins support vision, immunity, and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is important for DNA synthesis and especially beneficial during pregnancy.

items.title: Low‑calorie source of fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains glucosinolates
items.content: These compounds may have anti‑cancer effects by stimulating cellular detoxification.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to cruciferous vegetables.

items.title: High glucosinolate content
items.content: Excessive intake can irritate the gastrointestinal tract.

items.title: Interaction with anticoagulants
items.content: High vitamin K levels may reduce the effectiveness of blood‑thinning medications.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mustard greens can be eaten raw in salads, blended into smoothies, used as a garnish, or quickly sautéed with garlic and olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the greens in an airtight container in the refrigerator, where they stay fresh for 3–5 days. For longer storage, they can be frozen after blanching for 1–2 minutes.

pasta-whole-grain-with-cream-sauce-and-p.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Cream Sauce and Poultry, Ready‑to‑Heat

content.title: About
content.content: This is a ready‑to‑eat meal featuring whole‑grain pasta tossed in a smooth cream sauce and topped with pieces of poultry. The pasta is pre‑cooked al dente, the sauce is enriched with milk and cream, and the chicken is a lean source of protein. The dish is packaged in a single‑serve pouch that can be quickly heated in a microwave or on the stovetop.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain pasta provides more fiber and micronutrients than traditional white‑flour pasta.
The cream sauce is made from milk and cream, giving the dish a velvety texture.
Poultry used is typically chicken breast, making it a low‑fat protein source.
Ready‑to‑heat meals often contain small amounts of preservatives to extend shelf life.
Microwave heating usually takes 2–3 minutes, offering a convenient quick‑meal option.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta supplies fiber that supports healthy digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Chicken adds complete protein essential for muscle repair and immune function.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Both the pasta and poultry provide B1, B3, and B6 vitamins important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D in the sauce
items.content: The cream sauce contributes calcium and a modest amount of vitamin D, supporting bone health.

items.title: Low in trans fats
items.content: When produced correctly, the sauce contains no trans fats, making the meal more heart‑friendly.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: The cream sauce may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ready‑made meals often contain added salt; people monitoring sodium intake should account for this.

items.title: Heat safety
items.content: Insufficient heating can leave cold spots where bacteria might survive.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some packages use preservatives that may be undesirable for sensitive consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the pouch in the microwave (or on the stovetop) according to the label, stir to distribute the sauce evenly, and serve hot. Optionally garnish with fresh herbs, grated Parmesan, or additional vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened packages in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the product in a sealed container in the refrigerator and consume within 2–3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Meat or poultry‑filled pastries are baked goods made from yeast or puff pastry dough, stuffed with cooked, fried or stewed meat, poultry and sometimes vegetables. They are popular in Russia and CIS countries as a quick snack or part of a traditional meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Meat‑filled pastries appeared in Russian cuisine in the 19th century as street food.
The dough can be either yeasted or puff pastry, giving different textures.
Typical fillings include beef, pork, chicken or turkey, often with onion and spices.
During the Soviet era, large batches were produced and frozen for later reheating.
Some regions add a special meat broth to the filling to enhance flavor.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The meat filling provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat is rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The filling supplies B12, B6 and niacin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of dough and meat offers a quick source of energy, useful during physical activity.

items.title: Zinc content
items.content: Zinc from the meat supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Both the dough and meat can contain saturated fats, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Salt and preservatives
items.content: Commercial products often contain added salt and preservatives, which may be undesirable for people with hypertension.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat flour dough contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pastries can be eaten hot or warm, reheated in an oven, microwave or skillet. They are often served with mustard, sour cream or tomato sauce. For a lighter option, choose a whole‑grain dough version.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pastries in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a zip‑lock bag – they keep flavor for up to 2 months. Before eating, reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato French fries are thin strips or wedges of potato that are deep‑fried until golden and crispy. They are a staple side dish and snack in fast food, often served with a variety of dipping sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first documented recipe for fries appeared in Belgium in the late 19th century.
In the United States they are called "French fries" despite their Belgian origin.
There are many variations: classic, double‑fried, sweet potato, and herb‑seasoned versions.
The world’s largest single serving of fries weighed over 1.5 tons.
In some countries fries are served with mayonnaise, in others with ketchup or chili sauce.

items.title: Potassium source
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which supports heart and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: When cooked properly (not over‑fried) potatoes retain vitamin C, important for immunity.

items.title: Fiber
items.content: The skin of the potato provides dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: Fries supply fast‑acting carbohydrates, useful for intense physical activity.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Potatoes contain carotenoids and polyphenols with antioxidant properties.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Deep‑frying makes fries calorie‑dense and high in unhealthy fats, which can contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: Cooking at high temperatures can produce acrylamide, a potential carcinogen.

items.title: Salt
items.content: Excessive salting raises the risk of hypertension.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to potatoes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fries are served hot, typically in paper containers or boxes. They can be dipped in ketchup, mayonnaise, tartar sauce, cheese sauce, or seasoned with herbs and spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cooked fries are best eaten immediately. If needed, store them in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days; reheat in an oven to restore crispness.
